events/rabban-sauma-embassy-1287/summary: Rabban Sauma, an Uyghur or Önggüd monk of the Church of the East born near Khanbaliq, travelled west on pilgrimage and was sent by the Ilkhan Arghun as envoy to Constantinople, Rome, Paris and Gascony. He celebrated the Eucharist before Pope Nicholas IV and King Edward I — a reverse Marco Polo.
events/rabban-sauma-embassy-1287/consequ: Remarkable account of Europe from an Asian Christian
events/montecorvino-in-khanbaliq-1294/su: The Franciscan John of Montecorvino reached the Yuan capital, built churches, translated the Psalms and New Testament into a Mongolian or Uyghur language and baptised thousands. Made archbishop of Khanbaliq in 1307, he clashed with Church of the East clergy; the mission vanished after the Ming came to power in 1368.
events/avignon-papacy-1309/summary: Clement V, a Frenchman, settled the papal court at Avignon, where seven popes resided until Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377, urged by Catherine of Siena. The 'Babylonian Captivity' brought efficient administration but also accusations of French domination and fiscal greed.
events/avignon-papacy-1309/causes/0: Conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip IV of France
events/council-of-vienne-1311/summary: The fifteenth ecumenical council in the Catholic reckoning, convened by Clement V, suppressed the Knights Templar and defined that the rational soul is of itself and essentially the form of the human body, against teachings attributed to Peter John Olivi.
events/council-of-vienne-1311/causes/0: Pressure from Philip IV of France against the Templars
events/council-of-vienne-1311/consequenc: Made hylomorphic body-soul unity official Catholic teaching
events/eckhart-condemned-1329/title: Bull In agro dominico condemns propositions of Meister Eckhart
events/eckhart-condemned-1329/summary: On 27 March 1329 Pope John XXII, at Avignon, condemned 28 propositions drawn from Meister Eckhart’s works (17 as heretical, 11 as suspect), after a trial begun at Cologne in 1326. Eckhart had died c.1328 having submitted in advance to the Church’s judgement.
events/eckhart-condemned-1329/causes/0: Suspicion of Eckhart’s vernacular preaching on the soul’s union with God
events/eckhart-condemned-1329/causes/1: Concern about the Free Spirit movement
events/eckhart-condemned-1329/consequenc: Discouraged speculative vernacular mysticism; Tauler and Suso taught more cautiously
Eckhart’s reputation was revived by modern scholarship and interreligious dialogue
events/hesychast-controversy-1341/title: Hesychast controversy and the councils of Constantinople
events/hesychast-controversy-1341/summar: Barlaam of Calabria attacked the Athonite monks' hesychast prayer and claims to see the uncreated light of Tabor. Gregory Palamas defended them by distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies, in which believers truly participate. Councils in 1341, 1347 and 1351 vindicated Palamas.
events/hesychast-controversy-1341/longTe: Hesychasm ('stillness') was a method of contemplative prayer centred on the Jesus Prayer, sometimes linked to breathing and posture. Barlaam, a learned Greek from southern Italy, mocked it as 'navel-gazing' and argued that God can be known only indirectly. Palamas replied in the Triads that the vision of light granted to the disciples at the Transfiguration was a real, though not essential, participation in God — the divine energies are God himself in his self-giving, while his essence remains beyond participation. The controversy became entangled with the civil war between John VI Kantakouzenos and the regency of John V. The synods of 1341 and 1351 endorsed Palamite theology, which entered the Synodikon of Orthodoxy; Palamas was canonised in 1368. Orthodox theology sees the essence–energies distinction as safeguarding both divine transcendence and real deification (theosis). Many Catholic theologians historically viewed it as compromising divine simplicity, though recent scholarship and dialogue see more convergence.
events/hesychast-controversy-1341/conseq: Hesychasm spreads to the Slavic world
events/sergius-trinity-lavra-1345/title: Sergius of Radonezh founds the Trinity Lavra
events/sergius-trinity-lavra-1345/summar: Sergius of Radonezh founded a hermitage dedicated to the Holy Trinity in the forests north-east of Moscow, which grew into the greatest Russian monastery. His blessing of Prince Dmitri before the battle of Kulikovo (1380) made him a symbol of national revival.
events/sergius-trinity-lavra-1345/conseq: Rublev's Trinity icon painted for the Lavra
events/black-death-1347/summary: Bubonic plague killed perhaps a third to a half of the population of Europe and the Middle East. It provoked flagellant movements, pogroms against Jews accused of poisoning wells, intense devotion to death and judgement, and a shortage of clergy.
events/black-death-1347/causes/0: Plague carried along trade routes from Central Asia
events/black-death-1347/consequences/1: Penitential piety and art of the 'dance of death'
events/western-schism-1378/summary: The election of Urban VI in Rome was repudiated by French cardinals, who elected Clement VII in Avignon. Western Christendom divided its allegiance along political lines; a council at Pisa (1409) added a third pope. Constance ended the schism in 1417.
events/wycliffe-condemned-1382/title: Wycliffe condemned at the Blackfriars Synod
events/wycliffe-condemned-1382/summary: Archbishop Courtenay's 'Earthquake Synod' condemned propositions of John Wycliffe, who had attacked transubstantiation, clerical wealth and papal authority and urged the Bible as supreme authority. His followers produced the first complete English Bible; the Lollards were persecuted after 1401.
events/wycliffe-condemned-1382/causes/0: Wycliffe's Oxford teaching and royal patronage
events/timur-devastates-eastern-churches: Timur (Tamerlane) sacked Baghdad (1393, 1401), devastated cities across Persia, Mesopotamia, Georgia and Central Asia, and massacred populations including many Christians. Following earlier losses after the Ilkhans became Muslim, the Church of the East shrank to the mountains of Hakkari and northern Mesopotamia and to Kerala.
Near-disappearance of Christianity in Central Asia
Church of the East reduced to a mountain refuge
events/council-of-constance-1414/summary: The largest medieval council ended the Western Schism by deposing or receiving the resignations of three rival popes and electing Martin V. Its decree Haec sancta asserted conciliar authority over popes. It condemned Wycliffe and burned Jan Hus (1415) and Jerome of Prague despite Hus's safe-conduct.
events/council-of-constance-1414/longTex: Convened by Pope John XXIII (of the Pisan line) at the urging of Emperor Sigismund, Constance gathered bishops, theologians, princes and envoys from across Latin Christendom, voting by 'nations'. When John fled, the council declared in Haec sancta (1415) that it held its power immediately from Christ and that even a pope must obey it in matters of faith, schism and reform; Frequens (1417) required regular councils. Gregory XII resigned, Benedict XIII was deposed, and Martin V was elected in 1417. Hus, who came under imperial safe-conduct to defend himself, was condemned for Wycliffite errors and burned on 6 July 1415, sparking the Hussite revolution in Bohemia. Catholic theology later debated Haec sancta's authority: conciliarists saw it as binding; papal theologians, and finally Vatican I, rejected conciliar supremacy. Protestants regard Hus as a forerunner of the Reformation.
events/council-of-constance-1414/causes/: Calls for reform 'in head and members'
events/council-of-constance-1414/consequ: Execution of Hus and the Hussite wars
events/devotio-moderna-1418/title: Imitation of Christ and the Devotio Moderna
events/devotio-moderna-1418/summary: The Brethren of the Common Life, founded by Geert Groote at Deventer, cultivated inward piety among laypeople and clergy. The Imitation of Christ, attributed to Thomas à Kempis (c. 1418–27), became after the Bible perhaps the most widely read Christian book.
events/devotio-moderna-1418/consequences: Schools attended by Erasmus and others
Influence on Catholic and Protestant spirituality
events/hussite-revolution-1419/summary: Outraged by Hus's execution, Bohemian reformers demanded communion in both kinds (the chalice for the laity), free preaching and clerical poverty. After the defenestration of Prague (1419), Hussite armies under Jan Žižka defeated five crusades; the moderate Utraquists won recognition at Basel (1436), and the Unity of Brethren emerged in 1457.
events/hussite-revolution-1419/consequen: First successful reform church in the West
Unitas Fratrum, ancestor of the Moravians
events/council-of-florence-1439/summary: Emperor John VIII, Patriarch Joseph II and a large Greek delegation joined Pope Eugenius IV to negotiate reunion; the decree Laetentur caeli (6 July 1439) accepted the Filioque, purgatory, unleavened bread and papal primacy. Unions with Armenians (1439), Copts (1442) and others followed, and Ethiopian monks attended. Mark of Ephesus refused to sign, and the union was rejected in Constantinople and Moscow.
events/council-of-florence-1439/longText: Florence was the most serious medieval attempt to heal the East–West schism. The Byzantines, facing the Ottomans, hoped for military aid; theologians including Bessarion and Mark of Ephesus debated the Filioque for months, reaching a formula that the Spirit proceeds from the Father 'through the Son' understood as equivalent to 'and the Son'. The Decree for the Armenians summarised Latin sacramental theology (seven sacraments), and the Decree for the Jacobites (Copts) of 1442 contained the strict statement that no one outside the Catholic Church can be saved. Ethiopian delegates from Jerusalem attended, though no lasting union with Ethiopia followed. On their return, the Greek bishops faced popular hostility; Metropolitan Isidore of Kyiv was arrested in Moscow, which then elected its own metropolitan (1448). The union was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia only in December 1452, months before the city fell. Catholics count Florence as ecumenical; the Orthodox regard it as a false union, and Mark of Ephesus is venerated as a saint for his refusal.
events/council-of-florence-1439/causes/1: Conciliarist rivalry with the Council of Basel
events/council-of-florence-1439/conseque: Doctrinal statements on purgatory and sacraments
Templates for later Eastern Catholic unions
events/etchmiadzin-catholicosate-restore: Catholicosate restored at Etchmiadzin; Cilician line continues at Sis

The supreme Armenian see had followed the Armenian kingdom to Cilicia, residing at Sis from 1293. In 1441 an assembly at Etchmiadzin elected a new Catholicos there, while the Catholicos at Sis continued his own line, creating the two Catholicosates of All Armenians (Etchmiadzin) and of the Great House of Cilicia.
Fall of the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia (1375)
Desire to return the patriarchal seat to historic Armenia
Two catholicosates sharing one faith and liturgy
Cilician see moved to Antelias, Lebanon, in 1930 after the genocide
events/russian-autocephaly-1448/summary: Having rejected the union of Florence and imprisoned Metropolitan Isidore, Russian bishops elected Jonah metropolitan without Constantinople's consent, making the Russian church de facto autocephalous. After 1453 Moscow increasingly saw itself as the guardian of Orthodoxy — later expressed as the 'Third Rome' idea.
